subject: Renewal: GPU top-up, burst thresholds, and soft-fallback options
messages:
From: Samuel Park <sam.park@acme-ai.com>
To: lauren_bishop@redwood.ai
Date: 2027-07-12T09:13:00-07:00
Subject: Renewal: capacity increase and burst handling

Hi Lauren,

We’re starting our renewal discussion for the Dedicated pool that’s up at the end of July. Usage has steadily increased over the last 6 months and we’re seeing sustained peaks that push us beyond our reserved capacity. Two asks from our side: 1) increase reserved GPUs for steady-state inference and 2) clarify how burst/on-demand overflow will behave during those peaks.

Current snapshot: 48 vGPUs reserved (p3-equivalent), average sustained utilization ~75%, tail spikes up to ~140% for short windows (10-30m). We want predictable throughput for our 99th percentile traffic and to avoid request failures during major spikes.

Questions:
- Can you propose a renewal amendment that adds capacity and spells out overflow behavior (soft overflow vs hard cap)?
- Will you commit to throughput guarantees for the new reserved pools?
- What options exist for short-term burst (on-demand vs guaranteed extra reserved GPUs) and associated pricing/credits?

We’re aiming to finalize commercial terms and an ops playbook before July 20 so our procurement team can sign the renewal. I’ve CC’d our procurement lead, Liz Turner, for visibility.

Thanks — Sam

Samuel Park
Head of Platform Engineering
Acme.ai
From: lauren_bishop@redwood.ai
To: Samuel Park <sam.park@acme-ai.com>
Cc: Liz Turner <liz.turner@acme.ai>
Date: 2027-07-12T11:02:00-07:00
Subject: Re: Renewal: capacity increase and burst handling

Hi Sam — thanks for the clear summary. We can definitely support a combined reserved + burst approach and will propose an amendment that maps to your reliability needs. High-level options below; I attached a draft amendment and an SLO/throughput worksheet for your review.

Attachments: renewal_amendment_v1.pdf (draft commercial language), SLO-throughput-proposal.xlsx (throughput/latency matrix)

Option A — Reserved top-up + limited burst pool (recommended)
- Add 16 reserved GPUs to existing pool (steady-state uplift).
- Provision an 8-GPU burst pool (reserved but billed at lower committed rate when used); overflow beyond that falls back to on-demand instances (pay-as-you-go) subject to a soft threshold.
- We’ll document a soft overflow threshold at 110% of reserved capacity: beyond that, requests will be routed to on-demand with best-effort preemption rules and degraded throughput prioritization.
- Throughput guarantee: 99th percentile latency target for reserved capacity workloads; SLOs for burst usage are best-effort and captured in the amendment.

Option B — Hard cap + credit policy
- Add 24 reserved GPUs and enforce a hard cap (no on-demand spill).
- If capacity is reached, excess requests queue or receive graceful degradation.
- Predictable cost, but less flexible during unanticipated spikes.

Next steps I propose:
1) Dev and I validate the SLO/throughput assumptions in the attached spreadsheet.
2) If you prefer Option A, we finalize amendment language and propose a 12-month term for the added reserved GPUs (pricing tiers included in the PDF).
3) If Option B is preferred, we’ll run a short pricing model for the larger reserved commitment.

From an ops standpoint, we can implement the soft-overflow rules with these guardrails: a configurable preemption policy, warm standby on-demand pool with cold-start mitigation, and automatic routing to a lower-cost quantized variant if requested.

I’ll loop in Dev for technical confirmation on the preemption and fallback behavior.

Best,
Lauren Bishop
Senior Account Executive — Dedicated Accounts
Redwood Inference

Lauren/Sam — quick technical notes to make the SLOs concrete. Quoting Lauren below where helpful.

On preemption and overflow behavior (Option A):
- Soft threshold behavior: at 110% we start diverting new sessions to the on-demand spill pool. Existing reserved sessions continue until completion; new requests are load-shedded to on-demand.
- On-demand instances are provisioned from the same model family, with a safety margin for slightly higher latency (roughly +30–50ms p99 in our tests) due to differing GPU instance types and lack of warmed KV cache.
- We can enable prefix caching and KV warmup for a subset of sessions (cost tradeoff) — details in the attached workbook.

Throughput guarantees:
- We can offer a 99th-percentile latency target for reserved-capacity processed requests as a contractual SLO (example: p99 <= 320ms for generation requests under model family X at sequence length 256).
- For burst/on-demand we’ll provide a best-effort SLO and an operational playbook that lists fallback priorities (reserved -> quantized model variant -> on-demand -> queue).

Cost/ops implications:
- On-demand spill will incur higher variable cost, but we can include a monthly burst credit (e.g., 1,000 GPU-hours) as a renewal incentive.
- If Acme prefers predictable costs, Option B (higher reserved commit) is the cleaner financial path — but it increases committed spend.

I recommend Option A with these parameters: +16 reserved GPUs, +8 burst pool, soft threshold at 110%, and a one-month burst-credit (1,000 GPU-hours) baked into the renewal as a sign-on. That gives you flexibility without large upfront commitment.

Happy to run sample load traces against these knobs if you want concrete numbers for your procurement team.

— Dev
Principal Engineer, Serving Runtime
Redwood Inference

Please have Legal draft the final amendment language and include a DocuSign flow. Lauren — if you can confirm the exact pricing tier for +16 GPUs (list vs committed rate) I’ll sign off on the commercial redlines.
